claim: Cerebellar disease has long been known to result in disordered motor performance and motor learning.
source: Cerebellar disease has long been known to result in disordered motor performance and motor learning (Holmes, 1908; McCormick and Thompson, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to Holmes (1908) and McCormick and Thompson (1984).

claim: Cerebellar patients present with various degrees of cognitive, emotional and behavioral abnormalities.
source: Evidence has accumulated that cerebellar patients also present with various degrees of cognitive, emotional and behavioral abnormalities (Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schmahmann and Sherman (1998).

claim: The microscopic structure of the cerebellum is highly homogeneous.
source: Because the microscopic structure of the cerebellum is highly homogeneous, it is often assumed that the cerebellum performs one single neural operation (see Miall in Caligiore et al., 2017; Popa et al., 2014; Sokolov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caligiore et al. (2017), Popa et al. (2014), and Sokolov et al. (2017).

claim: The cerebellum is often assumed to perform one single neural operation.
source: Because the microscopic structure of the cerebellum is highly homogeneous, it is often assumed that the cerebellum performs one single neural operation (see Miall in Caligiore et al., 2017; Popa et al., 2014; Sokolov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Caligiore et al. (2017), Popa et al. (2014), and Sokolov et al. (2017).

claim: The most popular current hypothesis states that the cerebellum acts as, or is part of, a predictive device.
source: The most popular current hypothesis states that the cerebellum acts as, or is part of, a predictive device (Popa and Ebner, 2018 for recent review).
evidence: Supported by citation to Popa and Ebner (2018).

claim: In the motor domain, the cerebellum is crucially involved in prediction of the sensory consequences of motor commands via internal models.
source: In the motor domain, it is assumed that the cerebellum is crucially involved in prediction of the sensory consequences of motor commands thought to be achieved via internal models (Bastian, 2006; Miall et al., 1993; Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bastian (2006), Miall et al. (1993), and Wolpert et al. (1998).

claim: The difference between the predicted and actual sensory outcome results in a sensory prediction error used to adapt the internal model and subsequent motor behavior.
source: Assumedly, the difference between the predicted and actual sensory outcome results in a sensory prediction error used to adapt the internal model and subsequent motor behavior.
evidence: Based on theoretical reasoning about internal models and prediction errors.

claim: There is initial evidence that the cerebellum is involved in predictive control in the cognitive domain.
source: Although most studies have been performed in the motor domain, there is initial evidence that the cerebellum is involved in predictive control in the cognitive domain (Lesage et al., 2012; Lesage et al., 2017; Moberget et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lesage et al. (2012, 2017) and Moberget et al. (2014).

claim: The cerebellum is involved in acquisition of learned fear responses.
source: Fear conditioning was used as a model system because the cerebellum is involved in acquisition of learned fear responses (Lange et al., 2015; Maschke et al., 2002; Ploghaus et al., 1999; Sacchetti et al., 2002), and has known connections with several parts of the neural network underlying fear conditioning, including the limbic system (Badura et al., 2018; Blatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lange et al. (2015), Maschke et al. (2002), Ploghaus et al. (1999), and Sacchetti et al. (2002).

claim: The cerebellum has known connections with several parts of the neural network underlying fear conditioning, including the limbic system.
source: Fear conditioning was used as a model system because the cerebellum is involved in acquisition of learned fear responses (Lange et al., 2015; Maschke et al., 2002; Ploghaus et al., 1999; Sacchetti et al., 2002), and has known connections with several parts of the neural network underlying fear conditioning, including the limbic system (Badura et al., 2018; Blatt et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Badura et al. (2018) and Blatt et al. (2013).

claim: Prediction errors are thought to be the main drivers of associative fear learning.
source: Furthermore, prediction errors are thought to be the main drivers of associative fear learning (Holland and Schiffino, 2016; Rescorla and Wagner, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citations to Holland and Schiffino (2016) and Rescorla and Wagner (1972).

claim: The possible role of the cerebellum in aversive prediction error processing has largely been ignored in the fear conditioning literature.
source: In the fear conditioning literature, however, the possible role of the cerebellum in aversive prediction error processing has largely been ignored (Apps and Strata, 2015; Tovote et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Apps and Strata (2015) and Tovote et al. (2015).

claim: Previous studies focused on the role of the amygdala, insula, midbrain periaqueductal gray and striatum in aversive prediction error processing.
source: Previous studies focused on the role of the amygdala, insula, midbrain periaqueductal gray and striatum (Boll et al., 2013; Li et al., 2011; Li and McNally, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boll et al. (2013), Li et al. (2011), and Li and McNally (2014).

claim: During fear conditioning, participants learn to predict that the initially neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) is followed by an unpleasant unconditioned stimulus (US).
source: During fear conditioning, participants learn to predict that the initially neutral conditioned stimulus (CS) is followed by an unpleasant unconditioned stimulus (US).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of fear conditioning paradigms.

claim: Fear responses are elicited already at the time of CS presentation as a result of fear conditioning.
source: As a result, fear responses are elicited already at the time of CS presentation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of fear conditioning.

claim: The initial occurrence of the US is unexpected and has been considered as an error signal.
source: The initial occurrence of the US is unexpected and has been considered as an error signal (Taylor and Ivry, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Taylor and Ivry (2014).

claim: Participants learn within a very limited number of trials that the CS predicts the occurrence of the US, particularly if appropriate instructions are provided.
source: Participants learn within a very limited number of trials that the CS predicts the occurrence of the US, particularly if appropriate instructions are provided (Atlas et al., 2016; Tabbert et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atlas et al. (2016) and Tabbert et al. (2011).

claim: Cerebellar fMRI signals should be high during CS presentation if the cerebellum is involved in prediction of the US.
source: In case the cerebellum is involved in prediction of the US, cerebellar fMRI signals should be high during CS presentation.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the hypothesis about cerebellar involvement in prediction.

claim: Cerebellar activation should be increased at unexpected omission of the US if the cerebellum contributes to aversive prediction errors.
source: Thus, if the hypothesis is correct that the cerebellum contributes to aversive prediction errors, cerebellar activation should be increased at unexpected omission of the US (because of a partial reinforcement schedule).
evidence: Based on logical inference from the hypothesis about cerebellar involvement in prediction errors.

claim: During extinction, omission of the US becomes expected and cerebellar fMRI signals at the time of US omission should decrease.
source: During extinction, that is the repeated presentation of CS-only trials, omission of the US becomes expected and cerebellar fMRI signals at the time of US omission should decrease.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the hypothesis about cerebellar involvement in prediction errors.

claim: Cerebellar activations related to prediction of the US were found in accordance with the fMRI literature.
source: In accordance with the fMRI literature (Lange et al., 2015), we found cerebellar activations related to prediction of the US.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lange et al. (2015) and the study's own findings.

claim: Marked cerebellar activation was present during unexpected omission of the US.
source: In addition, marked cerebellar activation was present during unexpected omission of the US, which disappeared during extinction.
evidence: Based on the study's experimental data.

claim: Cerebellar activation during unexpected omission of the US disappeared during extinction.
source: In addition, marked cerebellar activation was present during unexpected omission of the US, which disappeared during extinction.
evidence: Based on the study's experimental data.

claim: The findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the cerebellum is involved in processing of aversive predictions and prediction errors.
source: Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the cerebellum is involved in processing of aversive predictions and prediction errors, and has to be added to the neural network underlying emotional associative learning.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's experimental data.

claim: The cerebellum has to be added to the neural network underlying emotional associative learning.
source: Our findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the cerebellum is involved in processing of aversive predictions and prediction errors, and has to be added to the neural network underlying emotional associative learning.
evidence: Based on inference from the study's experimental data.

claim: 27 participants underwent a differential fear conditioning and extinction paradigm using visual stimuli as CS and an unpleasant electrical shock as aversive US while acquiring 7T fMRI data.
source: While acquiring 7T fMRI data, 27 participants underwent a differential fear conditioning and extinction paradigm using visual stimuli as CS and an unpleasant, but not painful electrical shock as aversive US.
evidence: Based on the study's experimental design.

claim: After habituation and prior to acquisition, there was no difference in valence and arousal ratings of the CS+ and CS-.
source: After habituation and prior to acquisition, there was no difference in (hedonic) valence and (emotional) arousal ratings of the CS+ and CS- (Figure 2a).
evidence: Based on the study's behavioral data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: After acquisition, valence of the CS+ was rated less pleasant than that of the CS-.
source: After acquisition, valence of the CS+ was rated less pleasant than that of the CS-.
evidence: Based on the study's behavioral data.

claim: After acquisition, arousal to the CS+ was rated higher than that to the CS-.
source: Additionally, arousal to the CS+ was rated higher than that to the CS-.
evidence: Based on the study's behavioral data.

claim: Differences between CS+ and CS- ratings remained after extinction.
source: Differences between CS+ and CS- ratings remained after extinction, a finding that has been reported as resistance to extinction in evaluative conditioning research (e.g. Blechert et al., 2008; Vansteenwegen et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on the study's behavioral data and supported by citations to Blechert et al. (2008) and Vansteenwegen et al. (2006).

claim: ANOVA with repeated measures showed a significant difference within stimulus types and phases considering both valence and arousal (main effects: all p<0.002).
source: ANOVA with repeated measures showed a significant difference within stimulus types and phases (pre-acquisition, post-acquisition, post-extinction) considering both valence and arousal (main effects: all p<0.002).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the study's behavioral data.

claim: Valence and arousal ratings differed between stimulus type and phases (interaction stimulus type × phase: valence: F2,42 = 14.95, p<0.001; arousal: F2,42 = 15.30, p<0.001).
source: Valence and arousal ratings differed between stimulus type and phases (interaction stimulus type × phase: valence: F2,42 = 14.95, p<0.001; arousal: F2,42 = 15.30, p<0.001).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the study's behavioral data.

claim: Post hoc tests showed a significant difference between stimulus types after acquisition and after extinction (all p≤0.005; paired t-test), but not prior to acquisition (valence: p=0.781, arousal: p=0.125).
source: Post hoc tests showed a significant difference between stimulus types after acquisition and after extinction (all p≤0.005; paired t-test), but not prior to acquisition (valence: p=0.781, arousal: p=0.125).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the study's behavioral data.

claim: The mean US unpleasantness rating after acquisition was 6.9 (SD = 1.4) on a 9-point scale from 'not unpleasant' to 'very unpleasant'.
source: After acquisition, the mean US unpleasantness rating was 6.9 (SD = 1.4) on a 9-point scale from 'not unpleasant' to 'very unpleasant'.

claim: All participants were aware of CS-US contingencies after the acquisition phase.
source: All participants were aware of CS-US contingencies after the acquisition phase: The mean estimated probability that a CS+ was followed by an US was 70.0% (SD = 13.0%). All but one participant estimated a 0% probability of a CS- being followed by a US, with the remaining participant stating a 10% chance.

claim: The mean estimated probability that a CS+ was followed by a US was 70.0% (SD = 13.0%).
source: The mean estimated probability that a CS+ was followed by an US was 70.0% (SD = 13.0%).

claim: All but one participant estimated a 0% probability of a CS- being followed by a US, with the remaining participant stating a 10% chance.
source: All but one participant estimated a 0% probability of a CS- being followed by a US, with the remaining participant stating a 10% chance.
evidence: Based on the study's questionnaire data.

source: Participants stated that they became aware of CS-US contingencies after 2.9 min (SD = 1.2 min), or 2.6 (SD = 0.8) US events.

source: During habituation, second interval response (SIR) was not significantly different in CS+ and CS- trials (t21 = 0.708, p=0.487; paired t-test) (Figure 2c).

source: During fear acquisition, SIR was significantly higher in CS+ trials compared to CS- trials (Figure 2c).

claim: The difference in SIR between CS+ and CS- trials was most pronounced in the second half of the acquisition phase.
source: This difference was most pronounced in the second half of the acquisition phase.

claim: ANOVA with repeated measures showed a significant main effect of stimulus type (CS+ vs. CS-; F1,21 = 5.182, p=0.033) and block (early vs. late; F1,21 = 5.589, p=0.028) for SIR during acquisition.
source: ANOVA with repeated measures showed a significant main effect of stimulus type (CS+ vs. CS-; F1,21 = 5.182, p=0.033) and block (early vs. late; F1,21 = 5.589, p=0.028).

claim: The stimulus type by block interaction was not significant for SIR during acquisition (F1,21 = 1.409, p=0.249).
source: The stimulus type by block interaction was not significant (F1,21 = 1.409, p=0.249).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the study's SCR data.

source: During fear extinction, SIR related to the CS+ declined.

source: ANOVA with repeated measures showed a significant stimulus type by block interaction (F1,21 = 5.035, p=0.036).

source: SCRs in the unconditioned response (UR) window (i.e. the third interval response, TIR) were significantly higher in paired CS+ trials (US post CS+) compared to CS- trials (no-US post CS-) (F1,21 = 93.70, p<0.001) indicating a successful increase in SCR towards the electric shock (Figure 2d).

source: TIR was also significantly higher in unpaired CS+ trials (no-US post CS+) compared to CS- trials (no-US post CS-) during late acquisition (t21 = 3.72, p=0.001) but not early acquisition (t21 = 1.74, p=0.096), showing a higher US expectancy in US omission trials.

source: During extinction, TIR was not significantly different comparing stimulus types (no-US post CS+ vs. no-US post CS-; F1,21 = 3.46, p=0.077), blocks (early vs. late; F1,21 = 3.72, p=0.067) or their interaction (stimulus type by block; F1,21 = 0.02, p=0.878).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of the study's SCR data.

claim: A response towards the presentation and omission of the US during fear acquisition was demonstrated.
source: Taken together, we could show successful fear acquisition and extinction as well as a response towards the presentation and omission of the US during fear acquisition.
evidence: Based on the study's behavioral and SCR data.

claim: Widespread cerebellar activation was observed within the cerebellar vermis and both cerebellar hemispheres related to presentation of the aversive stimulus.
source: Widespread cerebellar activation was observed within the cerebellar vermis and both cerebellar hemispheres (Figure 3a; see also Table 1).
evidence: Based on the study's fMRI data shown in Figure 3a and Table 1.

source: Most prominent differential activations were found in the anterior and posterior vermis (local maxima in lobules I-IV, V) and the left hemisphere (that is ipsilateral to the presentation of the US; local maximum in Crus I).

source: Activation was not confined to the cerebellar cortex, but extended into the cerebellar nuclei (including dentate, interposed and fastigial nuclei bilaterally).

source: Cerebellar activation related to the CS+ was significantly higher in the lateral cerebellar hemispheres compared to activation related to the CS- (Figure 3b).

source: F-tests revealed no significant block effects (early vs. late) neither during acquisition nor during extinction (at p<0.05 FWE corrected level, based on the TFCE statistic).
